articles.title: Star Trek Talent Mourn Patrick Stewart: 'Captain Picard Stood For the Best of Us'
articles.summary: Sir Patrick Stewart’s friends and colleagues from the world of Star Trek have taken to social media to share their tributes to the late Jean-Luc Picard actor, who died Thursday at the age of 86 from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
articles.body:
Sir Patrick Stewart’s friends and colleagues from the world of Star Trek have taken to social media to share their tributes to the late Jean-Luc Picard actor, who died Thursday at the age of 86 from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

William Shatner, the iconic actor who portrayed Captain James T. Kirk in the original series, posted the following message on Facebook .

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote, referring to the death of Chekov actor Walter Koenig on Monday. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work. My heart goes out to Sunny and his family. He will be deeply missed.”

George Takei, who played Hikaru Sulu in the TV series and films featuring the original crew of the USS Enterprise, posted on Bluesky :

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity. Our hearts are heavy, indeed. Rest in the heavens, Captain.”

Stewart’s TNG co-stars Jonathan Frakes (Will Riker) and Will Wheaton (Wesley Crusher) also posted tributes online. Frakes wrote in an Instagram story, “Rest in peace, my friend.” Wheaton posted a photo of himself with Stewart, writing: “Godspeed, Captain.”

Akiva Goldsman, co-showrunner and co-creator on Star Trek: Picard, posted on X : “Safe Journey Dear Friend.”

Goldsman elaborated in a statement provided to Variety : “Patrick was not only a true lion of the profession, he was the rarest of alchemists, one who could literally turn the written word into flesh and blood. Patrick was kind, strong, fiercely intelligent, collaborative, vulnerable and wise. His Captain Jean-Luc Picard permanently expanded the universe of Star Trek without measure. He will be deeply missed by this one fan and by so many more.”

Stewart’s Picard co-star Jeri Ryan posted on Threads : “Ouch. This hurts, (heart emoji) Rest well, Patrick. (Vulcan hand salute emoji).”

Picard showrunner Terry Matalas posted a photo of Stewart smiling , with the caption: “Oh Captain, my Captain. This is how I’ll always remember you…”

Star Trek: Voyager’s Robert Picardo wrote : “Too much tragedy. Rest in peace, captain.”

Fellow Enterprise captain actor Anson Mount wrote in part: “Patrick was a friend. Not a close one, mind you, but it was a friendship, an “acquaintanceship” perhaps, that spanned more than half my life…“

Alex Kurtzman, the current overlord of the Star Trek Universe who brought Stewart back with the series Picard, posted photos of himself and Stewart together with the caption:

“This was the day Patrick announced his return to Star Trek. It’s hard, impossible really, to express how grateful I am to have shared this moment with him. Grateful in a “once in a career” kind of way.

Right from our first meeting, he made it known that the only reason to play Picard again was to break new ground. His challenge was clear: Picard needed to be the man we knew and loved, but also entirely different, just as Patrick himself was 30 years after last wearing the uniform. The world of the Federation had to feel fresh and mirror many of the big issues the world faces today, issues that he wanted to face as a human and an artist, which meant interrogating an ideal to expose something more honest.

He demanded truth. And in perhaps the trickiest high wire act, he wanted to reward fans with the nostalgia they would rightly demand, while subverting their expectations. More than anything, he wanted to be proud of the work because he knew that Jean-Luc Picard would be his legacy.

I am heartbroken, and also deeply proud, to know that legacy lives on as of today. A legacy that also includes being fearless when it came to speaking out about the things he believed in. A legacy that includes the way he loved his wife and cared for his family. A legacy that was so beautifully evident in the way he’d snuggle up to any pitbull he saw, and the way these supposedly fearsome creatures simply snuggled back.

He was magic. He was my colleague. He was my friend. He taught me what Star Trek was really about. And in the end, he was and always will be, my captain.”

articles.title: Bethesda Pays Tribute to Patrick Stewart for His Role in Oblivion, Fans Remember His Role in Games like Castlevania
articles.summary: Bethesda has paid tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart for his role in The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion after his death.
articles.body:
Bethesda has paid tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart for his role in The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion after his death.

Earlier today, it was announced that beloved actor Sir Patrick Stewart, best known for his roles in Star Trek and X-Men, died at 86 years old . The news came as a shock to many, and social media has been full of tributes to the actor. Many of his longtime collaborators, such as William Shatner, Kevin Feige, and Hugh Jackman all shared kind words about their time working with him.

Bethesda also offered up its own tribute by acknowledging the actor's death, calling him an "inspiration to us all." Stewart had a brief role in The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion as Emperor Uriel Septim VII, who is killed off at the very beginning of the game. Despite having minimal screen time, his character is the one who introduces you to the world of Cyrodiil and the looming threats that you will contend with.

Rest in peace to Sir Patrick Stewart — an emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all. Our thoughts are with his loved ones. — Bethesda Game Studios (@BethesdaStudios) October 29, 2026

Rest in peace to Sir Patrick Stewart — an emperor, a captain, and an inspiration to us all. Our thoughts are with his loved ones.

Despite having less than 10 minutes of screen time in the game, Bethesda put together a massive, overly-detailed document (reportedly as long as 90 pages) about the history and details of the Emperor. They thought that maybe they'd gone too far and worried that Stewart would ignore all of it, but executive producer Todd Howard stated that the actor was thrilled with the depth they had given the character and was excited to play him.

In a behind-the-scenes documentary about the making of Oblivion, developers gathered around in a room to listen to Stewart's first recordings for the game, gushing over how well he performed lines, some of which they feared would be cheesy. One developer was so enamored by Stewart's career that he carried around a picture of the actor in his wallet.

Fans of the game rallied on social media, saying that the actor was the perfect person to introduce players to the world in Oblivion.

"The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion would not have hit the same without the iconic introduction and prologue led by Patrick Stewart as Emperor Uriel Septim VII," said one fan .

"Despite only being in the game for the opening and tutorial, Patrick Stewart gave the intro of Oblivion immense gravitas that will never be forgotten and could not have been achieved my anyone else," echoed another .

Stewart had a pretty notable career in the video game industry outside of Oblivion. He reprised his Star Trek and X-Men characters for various video games over the years, but also did some pretty impactful voice work for games like Castlevania: Lords of Shadow.

Patrick Stewart's narration in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow Such an iconic voice — Radec (@realradec) October 29, 2026

Patrick Stewart's narration in Castlevania: Lords of Shadow Such an iconic voice

Stewart's family has encouraged fans and friends to donate to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: Gears of War: E-Day Reportedly Sold Over 400K Copies Across Console and PC a Month After Day-One Game Pass Launch
articles.summary: Sources tell The Verge that Gears of War: E-Day has sold over 400,000 copies across console and PC, and Game Pass is likely to blame.
articles.body:
Sources tell The Verge that Gears of War: E-Day has sold over 400,000 copies across console and PC, and Game Pass is likely to blame.

The latest entry in the Gears franchise released to critical acclaim earlier this month, drawing high scores from reviewers and fans alike. (IGN scored the game a 9 out of 10 , saying its “stellar story campaign is complemented by an excellent multiplayer suite.”)

However, it seems the title’s popularity isn’t translating to sales — at least, that’s according to a new figure reported by The Verge . Correspondent Tom Warren cited a source who estimated that 400,000 copies of the game have been sold in total across consoles and PC, which paints a grim figure considering the prestige of this particular release.

Many are pointing to Xbox Game Pass as the reason for this surprisingly low figure. The game was a day-one release on the service, and was available for early access five days before its official launch via a $30 Premium Edition Upgrade, meaning that total units sold are most certainly lower than those who accessed the title through Game Pass. (It’s also worth noting that most players were under the impression this would be a multiplatform release until Xbox revealed it as a console exclusive just four months before launch.)

Data from Alinea Analytics appears to corroborate this thought. As laid out in an October 9 post from the research firm’s head of market analysis, Rhys Elliott, an estimated 1.7 million players accessed E-Day using their Game Pass subscription, rather than buying a copy.

Elliott figured that of those 1.7 million players, likely 722,000 paid for the Premium upgrade, with the game prompting an additional 250,000 Premium upgrades between October 1 and the game’s full release on October 6.

Gears Of War: E-Day at 4k Max Settings Battles in Kalona GFN

As told by Elliott at the time of his post, “E-Day sold 62,000 copies on Xbox against 722,000 Premium upgrades, so for every one copy sold on Xbox, nearly 12 Game Pass upgrades were sold.” He surmised that Xbox accounted for nearly three-quarters of the game’s total revenue, but said that despite these seemingly low numbers, nearly 950K likely paid for the game in some way — just not by outright purchasing an actual copy.

These E-Day figures follow news that Xbox Game Pass might be receiving a major overhaul that could let subscribers pick which features they want to actually pay for. As told by Fortune , this would include "add-ons for console-only games, cloud gaming, and multiplayer, with the system operating on a tiered structure, according to people familiar with the strategy."

It’s a turbulent time for Xbox, which is still in the midst of a massive restructuring . A total of 3,200 employees are expected to lose their jobs at the company, as told by CEO Asha Sharma this summer. This restructuring has also resulted in the divestment of several game studios, including Arkane Lyon, who now has until December 13, 2026 to find a buyer and save its highly-anticipated Blade game .

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: Caitlin Clark Would Have Saved This Horrendous WNBA Finals! The League Is Missing Its Biggest Star
articles.summary: The WNBA Finals have been crying out for excitement, and one of the biggest names in the sport has been watching from the sidelines. Caitlin Clark’s absence...
articles.body:
The WNBA Finals have been crying out for excitement, and one of the biggest names in the sport has been watching from the sidelines. Caitlin Clark's absence has left a massive hole in the postseason, and it's hard not to wonder how much more entertaining this series would have been with her on the floor.

Instead of getting the star power, offensive fireworks and nonstop attention Clark brings, fans have been left watching a Finals series filled with frustrating shooting performances, ugly offensive stretches and constant conversations about the officiating.

The Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries deserve credit for making it this far, but the overall product has been difficult to watch at times. Game 5 was a perfect example, with Atlanta managing just 55 points in a loss. The shooting struggles and lack of offensive rhythm made for a brutal night of basketball.

Clark could have changed the entire feel of this series. Her playmaking, deep shooting range and ability to create offense out of nothing bring a different level of excitement. She attracts attention every time she steps on the court, and her presence would have given the Finals another major storyline for fans to follow.

Her absence has also made the league's handling of its biggest stars a bigger talking point. Clark dealt with controversial officiating and physical play during the first round before her season ended, leaving fans wondering what the postseason might have looked like if she had stayed healthy.

Of course, nobody can guarantee Clark would have transformed every game or fixed the shooting struggles of the teams playing in the Finals. But there is no denying that having one of the league's most recognizable and exciting players competing for a championship would have brought another level of attention to the series.

The WNBA needed its biggest stars on the biggest stage. Instead, Clark has been watching from home while the Finals have struggled to consistently deliver the kind of basketball fans expected.

And with the series heading to a winner-take-all Game 7, the league is left wondering just how much bigger this moment could have been with Caitlin Clark involved.

articles.title: How Angel Reese’s playmaking helped the Dream send the WNBA Finals to Game 7
articles.summary: ATLANTA — Heading into Game 6 between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries, it seemed like all anyone could talk about was the matinee timing of the...
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Heading into Game 6 between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries, it seemed like all anyone could talk about was the matinee timing of the potential WNBA Finals clincher. How would Thursday's 12:30 p.m. ET tipoff affect the players' body clocks, the fans' ability to attend the game, or the broadcast viewing audience?

For Angel Reese, the upside was pretty clear. "The sun peeked out a little bit more today," Reese said. "(It) gave us a little bit of an opportunity to see Game 7."

Reese has been the bellwether for Atlanta in the finals. When she plays well and exerts her will, the Dream win. When she is stifled or rushed and her impact isn't felt — well, that's why this series is going to seven games.

The third-year big, who will finish her first season with Atlanta on Saturday, is the Dream's emotional engine. Her enthusiasm seeps into her teammates; her confidence reminds them why they're one of the last two squads standing. After the Game 5 loss that put Atlanta down 3-2, Reese was the one proclaiming, "I would still believe in our team; (I) still believe we can win this."

But more importantly, Reese is the fulcrum for the team's success. The Dream need her force on the court: the bone-crushing screens to create space for shooters, the rim runs to collapse the defense, the power drives to the basket. When Reese is passive, it trickles down. When she's aggressive, that spreads even faster.

In an 80-69 Game 6 victory , Reese did the things that had worked for her earlier in the series, grabbing and going after defensive rebounds without getting the ball to a guard. Not all of those forays led to points for Atlanta, but they increased the overall tempo, which had slowed to a crawl in the previous two games.

She was her usual dominant self on the glass and contributed to an 11-4 advantage in second-chance points for the Dream. She attacked Kiah Stokes more often on drives than in the post, benefiting from Atlanta's improved spacing.

The Dream also put the ball in Reese's hands more often to start Game 6, and she finished with six assists, a series-high for her. Golden State's ball pressure had sped up the Dream in their prior two losses, so Atlanta adjusted. One frequent set stationed Reese in the middle of the floor with a shooter (usually Rhyne Howard or Allisha Gray) in one corner and the other three Atlanta players involved in a weakside action. That let Reese's playmaking shine. She found Gray on the wing for Atlanta's first 3 of the game, then Naz Hillmon on the ensuing possession at the top of the key.

For a Dream team that shot 10 of 49 from 3-point range over the previous two contests, all they needed was to see the ball go through the net a couple of times. That opened the floodgates for Jordin Canada, Gray and Howard to hit four 3-pointers in the span of five possessions. Atlanta blew open the game in the first quarter, taking a 17-point lead that wouldn't drop to single digits until 1:15 remained in the game.

Gray made five 3s to lead Atlanta with 23 points, and Howard added four triples for 21. Both players had their best scoring games of the finals on Thursday.

"We played with a different spacing and pace," Dream coach Karl Smesko said. "In truth, it's how we are supposed to play. In the first half, you saw it. The catch and ready to shoot, the pace of one action leading directly into another action, to getting the ball out and going and putting some pressure on them in transition. It's just the way that we are capable of playing and the way we're supposed to play."

Reese got into the 3-point party herself after lamenting her failure to take any 3s in Game 5. She has shot well from long range during the postseason, making 38.5 percent of her triples on 2.4 attempts per game, but she turned down a couple of open looks amid Atlanta's overall shooting struggles.

Reese's shooting may not meaningfully change the way opponents defend the Dream, but her 3s are backbreakers. Atlanta is 16-0 when she makes a 3, and the other Dream players are well aware of that stat. She let it fly Thursday, with her first shot attempt coming from beyond the arc. Reese finished with 15 points and 14 rebounds on 2-of-8 shooting from 3 and 5-of-18 from the floor.

"We tell her she needs to shoot, and we kept drawing up plays so she could shoot the ball," Howard said postgame.

"It definitely was tough, and always frustrating, especially for 3s, because they keep telling me to shoot and I don't like when I'm not making the shots," Reese said. "But my teammates still trust and pass it to me. I'm also really, really grateful to them for always putting confidence into me."

Even in victory, the shooting efficiency wasn't there for Reese. She made 30 percent of her shots from inside the arc and committed six turnovers. Still, her shot creation and distribution gave Atlanta the early push it needed to force Game 7, which is set for 8 p.m. ET Saturday in San Francisco.

"It was just a mental mindset of me just being able to go out there and try to lead the team as best I can, no matter how ugly it could be, as long as we came out with the win," Reese said. "I just wanted to do whatever it took to win."
